overview: Ancient Hadramawt was a South Arabian kingdom centred on Shabwa, connected with oasis farming and Arabian trade. Its recorded history begins before the map’s 323 BCE start, and independence ended around 300 CE, before the imported 500 cutoff. The outline is seriously incomplete: it includes eastern territory toward Dhofar but omits Shabwa and the port of Qana to the west. This card concerns the ancient kingdom and its communities, not the separate medieval “Hadramaut” record.

periods.title: A kingdom before the imported start
periods.summary: Hadramawt is mentioned around 700 BCE. The map’s 323 BCE beginning does not mark its foundation.

periods.title: Ports and regional competition
periods.summary: Sumhuram and Qana connected the kingdom with Indian Ocean commerce. Royal building and conflict shaped its cities.

periods.title: After political independence
periods.summary: Settlement and maritime activity continued after annexation. Qana’s excavated history reaches beyond this map’s final year.

sections.title: Incense, shipping and a working port

items.text: Frankincense is aromatic tree resin, rather than a flower or a manufactured perfume. Eastern communities collected it in Hadramawt and Dhofar, and merchants carried it toward the Mediterranean and other markets. People burned it in worship and used aromatic materials in perfumes and preparations. Its value linked rural producers with rulers, temples, traders and distant customers.

The coastal outpost of Sumhuram, at Khor Rori in today’s Oman, gathered incense for shipping toward Qana. From there, cargo could enter wider networks reaching the Mediterranean. Sea transport developed alongside older land routes; the kingdom’s commercial story was more complicated than one uninterrupted camel caravan crossing Arabia.

At Qana, excavators uncovered houses and a storeroom, together with hundreds of bronze coins and pottery from Africa and the Mediterranean. These finds help reconstruct a functioning port where people lived, stored goods and made transactions. Imported pots demonstrate connections, but they do not identify the nationality of every person who used them.

Not everyone lived in an imposing tower house. Two homes excavated beside an oasis canal near Shabwa had mudbrick walls joined with pink mortar, sometimes finished with red plaster. Their ground floors contained storage rooms and kitchens. Coins from the second and third centuries CE help place these households within the ancient kingdom’s later history.

Those canal-side kitchens yielded cooking pots, jars, bowls, grinding stones and mortars. These are practical traces of preparing and keeping food. Their inhabitants needed space for work and supplies as well as shelter. A jar full of provisions could matter more to supper than all the splendid decoration in the royal palace.

Around Shabwa, old field boundaries and waterworks survive across areas now largely uncultivated. Pierre Gentelle’s survey combined aerial photographs with walking the ground, mapping features and collecting pottery and other finds. This joined landscape evidence with objects: an abandoned channel could help explain a city just as much as a carved inscription.

Farmers diverted seasonal floodwater into channels and distributed it among prepared fields. The water also deposited fertile silt, slowly raising ground levels and complicating irrigation. Early in the third century CE, King Ili’azz Yalut commissioned a sluice at a new canal’s head. Keeping water useful required repeated adjustments, not simply building a dam once.

sections.title: Building upward and working with local materials

items.text: Shabwa’s substantial houses stood on stone platforms, with upper storeys built using timber frames and mudbrick. Some rubble-filled foundation compartments were once mistaken for tombs or storage rooms. Examining how the walls fitted together changed the interpretation: a solid compartment supporting a building is not necessarily a room anyone could enter.

Staircases linked the upper floors. In the royal palace, surviving mudbrick steps and traces of timber-supported flights help archaeologists reconstruct movement through the building. Building 72 had an unusual stone staircase. Upper rooms and household arrangements are partly reconstructed; the remains do not tell us that ancient men and women always occupied separate floors.

Roof water needed a way down without soaking the walls. Excavators found gutters with bull-head spouts at Shabwa. Their decoration gave an animal face to a useful building part. Ancient architecture included such small practical decisions as well as monumental entrances and impressive heights.

Shabwa also stood on a salt dome that was mined in antiquity. Salt supplied a local resource and a source of income alongside the city’s trade connections. The capital’s economy therefore involved extraction and work in its immediate surroundings, as well as luxury goods arriving from far away.

A calcite incense burner associated with Shabwa shows a rider seated in front of a camel’s hump. The museum dates it tentatively to the third century CE. It stands 32 centimetres high, yet its shallow top holds only about 30 millilitres. The grand-looking carving had a surprisingly small working bowl.

At Sumhuram, the temple dedicated to Sin included an altar, basins interpreted as places for ritual washing, and a kitchen for preparing ritual meals. Worship could involve water, food and shared activity as well as incense. These installations belong to a sanctuary; they are not evidence of bathrooms or healthcare in every home.

Sumhuram’s furnaces, crucibles and ironworking waste show that the port also contained workshops. Archaeologists recovered many stone and bronze tools. Cargo did not simply pass through an empty warehouse beside the sea: residents made and repaired things in a settlement with its own working life.

sections.title: A written place name and a metalworker’s correction

items.text: A bronze plaque from Sumhuram preserves “𐩨𐩪𐩣𐩠𐩧𐩣”, b-S¹mhrm, meaning “at Sumhuram”. These are modern typeset Old South Arabian letters for a Hadramitic phrase in line 3 of inscription KR 11. Excavated in 2013, the dedication is provisionally dated to the first century CE from its floor context and letter forms.

That plaque was made by lost-wax casting and had already been repaired in antiquity. The maker also misjudged the space for its inscription: the last two letters of the donor’s name were added at the text’s end. Even an expensive bronze dedication could need the ancient equivalent of squeezing in a forgotten word.

A sack of Shabwa around 225 to 230 CE badly damaged the royal palace. Hadramawt’s rulers subsequently returned and rebuilt above surviving foundations. The kingdom survived this interruption. Fourth-century Himyarite occupation belongs to a later political phase.

At Qana, painted and inscribed Greek fragments date to the fourth century CE, after the kingdom had lost independence. Excavation also shows that the port lasted until the beginning of the Islamic era. A political border could change while buildings, shipping connections and the daily work of a coastal community continued.

ending.text: Hadramawt lost its independence to Himyar around 300 CE, following regional warfare. This occurred before the map’s 500 endpoint. Its communities did not vanish together: Qana continued into the beginning of the Islamic era. The later medieval Hadramaut record concerns a different political setting, not an uninterrupted continuation of this ancient kingdom.
